title: FastAPI: middleware, dependencies and async
description: Starlette middleware ordering, dependencies as cross-cutting tools, CORS, async versus plain def endpoints, thread-pool limits, gather timing and server-sent events.
source: Starlette middleware documentation; FastAPI documentation (middleware, concurrency and async/await, custom response); AnyIO thread limiter documentation; Python asyncio documentation
seriesDescription: Python and FastAPI interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Python/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Python only: nothing here mixes in Java.

questions.prompt: Three Starlette middleware A, B and C are added to an app in that order with app.add_middleware(A), then B, then C. At which position (1 = first to see an incoming request) does A's pre-request code run?
questions.explanation: Middleware added last is outermost, so a request goes C, B, A. Responses unwind A, B, C. Verified with @app.middleware logging.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI HTTP middleware that measures how long the request took (time.perf_counter) and sets the response header X-Process-Time.
questions.model:
@app.middleware("http")
async def add_time(request, call_next):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = str(time.perf_counter() - start)
    return response
questions.explanation: Pure ASGI middleware or add_middleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware) subclasses are equivalent. Note BaseHTTPMiddleware has caveats with streaming responses and contextvars.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI dependency require_key that reads the X-API-Key header and raises HTTPException 401 unless it equals "secret", then attach it to a router so every route needs it.
questions.starter: from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, Header, HTTPException
questions.explanation: Dependencies are the FastAPI answer to per-route auth: they run inside routing, know path params and can use other dependencies. Verified: missing header gives 422, wrong key 401, right key 200.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A FastAPI dependency can short-circuit a request by raising HTTPException.
questions.reason: Dependencies run only after all middleware has already returned a response.

whys.c: Correct: A is true, but R is false because dependencies run inside route handling, i.e. within the middleware stack.

questions.explanation: Order: middleware (outer) then routing then dependencies then handler, and back out through middleware again.

questions.prompt: An async def FastAPI endpoint calls time.sleep(2) inside its body. A single uvicorn worker receives 3 requests at the same instant. About how many seconds until the last client gets its response?
questions.explanation: time.sleep blocks the event loop, so requests are served one after another: 3 x 2 = 6. With a plain def the work runs in the threadpool, giving roughly 2, and await asyncio.sleep(2) also gives roughly 2.

questions.prompt: Your FastAPI endpoint calls a synchronous, blocking database driver. Which declaration is the safest choice?

options.text: A plain def endpoint, so FastAPI runs it in a threadpool.
options.why: The sync code runs off the event loop, so other requests keep flowing.

options.text: async def, with the blocking call made directly inside the endpoint body.
options.why: The blocking call freezes the whole event loop while it runs.

options.text: async def and sprinkle await in front of the driver call.
options.why: Awaiting a non-awaitable fails; it does not make the driver non-blocking.

options.text: async def plus a global asyncio lock.
options.why: A lock serialises requests and does not stop the loop from blocking.

questions.explanation: Use async def only with async libraries (asyncpg, httpx.AsyncClient) or offload with run_in_threadpool.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI GET /events endpoint that streams server-sent events: an async generator that yields "data: tick N" for N = 0, 1, 2 (with the SSE blank-line terminator), wrapped in a streaming response of the right media type.
questions.explanation:
Each SSE event ends with a blank line. Verified: output is 'data: 0

data: 1

' with content type text/event-stream. Browsers consume it with EventSource, which reconnects automatically.

questions.prompt: A plain def FastAPI endpoint runs time.sleep(1) in the default threadpool, which allows 40 worker threads. One uvicorn worker receives 100 requests at the same instant. About how many seconds until the last response?
questions.explanation: Sync endpoints run in AnyIO's threadpool with a default limit of 40 threads, so the 100 requests go in batches of 40, 40 and 20: 3 seconds (measured 3.3 s locally). The same 100 requests to an async def with asyncio.sleep(1) would take about 1 s.

questions.prompt: True or false: in FastAPI, when a dependency raises HTTPException(401), the resulting 401 response still passes back through your @app.middleware("http") function, so a header set there is added to it.

options.why: Correct: HTTPException is converted to a response by Starlette's exception handling, which sits inside user middleware.
The 401 is a normal response object by the time it unwinds, so middleware still sees it; only unhandled exceptions (500) bypass this.

questions.explanation: ExceptionMiddleware sits inside the middleware you add, so HTTPException responses unwind through it (verified locally: 401 carried the middleware's header). Truly unhandled exceptions are turned into 500 by the outermost ServerErrorMiddleware.

questions.prompt: Inside an async def FastAPI route, call the blocking, synchronous function crunch(data) without freezing the event loop, by running it in a worker thread, and return the result.
questions.model:
@app.post("/crunch")
async def crunch_route(data: dict):
    result = await run_in_threadpool(crunch, data)
    return result
questions.explanation: asyncio.to_thread(crunch, data) is equivalent. Both use a thread pool, so CPU-bound pure-Python work still competes for the GIL; use a process pool or a task queue for heavy CPU work.
questions.starter:
from fastapi.concurrency import run_in_threadpool
import asyncio

questions.prompt: An async def route runs await asyncio.gather(a(), b(), c()), where each coroutine does await asyncio.sleep(0.5). About how many milliseconds does the route take?
questions.explanation: gather starts the three coroutines together and the sleeps overlap, so the total is about 0.5 s (verified: 0.50 s). Awaiting them one after another would take about 1500 ms.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: An async def route that awaits asyncio.sleep(2) does not stop the server from handling other requests during those 2 seconds.
questions.reason: await hands control back to the event loop until the awaited operation finishes.

whys.a: Correct: while one request waits, the loop runs other tasks.
whys.b: Wrong: R is exactly the mechanism.

questions.explanation: This is why async shines for I/O-bound work and why one blocking call such as time.sleep breaks it.

questions.prompt: Match each Starlette or FastAPI component with what it does.

right.text: Turns unhandled exceptions into a 500 response; it is the outermost layer
Converts HTTPException and registered exception handlers into responses
Answers preflight requests and adds Access-Control-* headers
Compresses large responses for clients that accept gzip
Validates the request body against a Pydantic model
Starts background tasks after the response

questions.explanation: Request validation happens inside routing, not in middleware. Custom middleware you add sits between ServerErrorMiddleware and ExceptionMiddleware.

questions.prompt: Add Starlette's CORS middleware to a FastAPI app so that only the origin https://app.example.com may call the API, with only the methods GET and POST.
questions.explanation: Verified: a request with Origin: https://app.example.com receives the matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. Never combine allow_origins=["*"] with allow_credentials=True.
questions.starter:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
app = FastAPI()

questions.prompt: Only the /admin routes need an API-key check, and the check needs the path parameters of the matched route. Which tool fits best?

options.why: Middleware runs before routing, is global and cannot see matched route parameters.

options.text: A startup hook in lifespan that registers the allowed keys.
options.why: Lifespan runs once per process, not per request.

options.text: A background task started after each response is sent.
options.why: It would run after the response, far too late to reject the request.

options.text: A dependency attached to an APIRouter for /admin.
options.why: Correct: dependencies run inside routing, so they see matched parameters and apply to a subset.

questions.explanation: Use middleware for concerns that apply to everything (request id, timing, compression) and dependencies for per-route or per-router rules such as authentication and permissions.

questions.prompt: True or false: calling time.sleep(2) inside an async def route blocks every other request handled by that worker for 2 seconds.

options.why: Correct: time.sleep does not yield to the event loop, so the whole loop is frozen.
The loop is single-threaded; a blocking call inside a coroutine stops all coroutines on it.

questions.explanation: Use await asyncio.sleep(2) in coroutines, or a plain def route, which FastAPI runs in a thread pool.

questions.prompt: True or false: FastAPI runs async def routes in a thread pool, which is why blocking calls inside them are harmless.

options.why: Wrong: async def routes run directly on the event loop.
Correct: only plain def routes (and sync dependencies) go to the thread pool; async def routes run on the loop itself.

questions.explanation: This is the root of the classic mistake of putting blocking database calls inside async def routes.
